newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma turns wanted drug suspect over to Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Burma turns wanted drug suspect over to Thailand.

text.p: Burma's military government said on Saturday it had handed over to Thai authorities an accused drug trafficker wanted in the United States for allegedly masterminding the biggest heroin haul in U.S. history.
A Burmese government statement said Li Yun Chung, alias Phongsak Rogianasakul, was handed over to Thai officials on Saturday. He had fled to Burma after jumping bail in Thailand in March.
The Burmese government in March had denied it was sheltering Li -- the main suspect in a drug haul worth up to $122 million.
Thai authorities said in March they believed Li had fled to Burma shortly after being granted bail by a Thai judge in early February.
At the time United States complained about the Thai court decision to grant bail to Li, who has a Thai identity card.

Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council said it regarded total eradication of narcotic drugs as a national task and its decision to hand over Li to Thailand was aimed at boosting the region's fight against drug trafficking.

The Bangkok Post on Saturday quoted Thai official sources as saying that Li, who was awaiting a Thai decision on his extradition to the United States when he jumped bail, had been captured by Burmese officials at the Burmese border town of Techilek.
Li was indicted by a New York court in May 1996 in connection with the largest heroin haul ever in the United States -- the seizure in 1991 of 486 kg (nearly 1,070 lb) in Hayward, California.
Drugs officials put the U.S. street value between $180,000 to $250,000 per kg, making the haul worth $87.5 million to $122 million.
Li was the second major drug suspect wanted in the United States who was seeking refuge in Burma.

Opium warlord Khun Sa, also wanted on drugs charges in the United States, is living in Rangoon after surrendering to Burmese troops last year. Burma has vowed not to extradite him and said the government would deal with him in its own way.

Li's handover to the Thai authorities occurred the same day Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh completed his two-day official visit to Rangoon where he discussed border cooperation and joint narcotics suppression.
U.S. drug officials have accused Burma, which they say is the largest producer of opium, of not doing enough to fight the scourge of narcotics.
The officials estimate that more than half of the heroin on the streets in the United States originates in Burma. Heroin is a refined form of opium.
